title: SQL and PostgreSQL for Frontend Developers
description: Query relational data safely and understand joins, aggregation, NULL, constraints, and access control.
learningOutcomes: Write SELECT, JOIN, subquery, and aggregate queries.
Handle NULL's three-valued logic, including NOT IN edge cases.
Explain join grain, constraints, transactions, and parameterized values.
Distinguish frontend filtering from trusted authorization.

blocks.text: Think in relations before writing SQL

Tables contain rows and columns; keys connect related rows and constraints protect invariants. SQL is declarative: describe the result and let the database choose a plan. Understand the relationship between records before joining tables or adding aggregates.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.active = TRUE
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(o.id) >= 2
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 20;

steps.title: Join related tables
steps.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves customers without matching orders. COUNT(o.id) counts matched order IDs; COUNT(*) counts joined rows.

steps.title: Filter rows and groups at different stages
steps.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregate values are calculated.

steps.title: Sort and limit results
steps.explanation: LIMIT bounds the result; stable pagination often also requires a unique ordering key.

blocks.text: NULL, constraints, and safe query construction

Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test SQL NULL; it is not an ordinary value and = NULL is not the correct predicate. PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK and NOT NULL constraints enforce integrity beyond the frontend. Parameterize user-supplied values through a trusted API/server instead of concatenating them into SQL.

blocks.title: Do not expose database credentials to the browser
blocks.text: Database access should go through a trusted server or a platform whose public client access is restricted by enforced row-level security. A frontend filter does not restrict which rows an attacker can request.
Read the query in logical stages

SQL is declarative: the text is written SELECT-first, but a useful mental model is FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. This explains why a SELECT alias is usually unavailable in WHERE, and why filtering an aggregate belongs in HAVING. The database optimizer may execute a different physical plan; logical order is for reasoning, not a promise about execution.

blocks.code:
SELECT id, email
FROM customers
WHERE active = TRUE
  AND created_at >= DATE '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 20;

steps.title: Choose rows from a relation
steps.explanation: FROM names the relation; WHERE keeps rows that satisfy the predicate. Multiple predicates can be composed with AND/OR—use parentheses when precedence would be unclear.

steps.title: Sort deterministically and bound the result
steps.explanation: ORDER BY sorts after filtering. Adding id as a tie-breaker makes equal timestamps deterministic; LIMIT without an order does not promise which rows appear.

blocks.text: NULL uses three-valued logic

A predicate involving NULL can be TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. WHERE retains only TRUE, so comparisons such as score > 0 silently discard NULL rows. Use IS NULL for missing values and COALESCE only when substituting a deliberate display/calculation default. Watch NOT IN: if its set contains NULL, the result may be UNKNOWN for every candidate; a correlated NOT EXISTS is often safer.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.id
FROM customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM blocked_customers AS b
  WHERE b.customer_id = c.id
);

steps.title: Correlate the inner query to the current row
steps.explanation: The inner query tests whether a matching blocked-customer row exists for this customer.

steps.title: Keep only rows with no match
steps.explanation: NOT EXISTS is boolean and avoids the NULL trap of NOT IN. If customer_id can itself be NULL, decide explicitly whether such rows should be included.

blocks.text: Join grain and row multiplication

Before joining, state what one row represents on each side. A one-to-many join repeats the parent row; joining two one-to-many tables can multiply both child sets. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) may correct a count, but it is not a universal repair for sums or incorrect data modeling. Aggregate each child relation to the required grain first when needed.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.id,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT r.id) AS reviews
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN reviews AS r ON r.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id;

steps.title: Notice the two independent one-to-many joins
steps.explanation: A customer with two orders and three reviews produces six joined rows before grouping.

steps.title: Count identities, not multiplied rows
steps.explanation: DISTINCT avoids double-counting these IDs. For sums or larger queries, pre-aggregate orders and reviews in separate subqueries/CTEs instead of relying on DISTINCT.

blocks.text: Subqueries and conditional results

Use EXISTS when the question is whether a related row exists; use a join when columns from the related relation are needed. A scalar subquery must return at most one row. CASE expresses conditional values in the result and can make reports clearer, but it does not replace filtering or constraints.

blocks.code:
SELECT id,
       CASE WHEN total >= 100 THEN 'large' ELSE 'standard' END AS order_size
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1;

blocks.text: Пусть ограничения защищают данные

PRIMARY KEY identifies a row; FOREIGN KEY requires a related parent row; NOT NULL rejects missing values; UNIQUE prevents duplicate keys; CHECK enforces a row-level rule. Constraints protect writes from every client, unlike form validation. Choose ON DELETE behavior deliberately: cascading deletion can be correct for dependent data, but dangerous for shared records.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  total NUMERIC(12, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  status TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (customer_id, created_at)
);

blocks.title: A constraint is part of the data contract
blocks.text: Application checks improve feedback; database constraints are the final integrity gate. Handle constraint errors as expected outcomes, not impossible crashes.
Use transactions for related writes

A transaction groups database changes so they succeed or fail together. Keep it short, check the returned rows, and roll back when a required step fails. A transaction does not automatically solve concurrent updates: use a suitable constraint, lock, or isolation level for the invariant.

steps.title: Guard the update in the database
steps.explanation: The predicate prevents a negative quantity in this statement; RETURNING lets the caller verify whether a row changed.

steps.title: Commit or roll back based on the result
steps.explanation: The comment is an application decision point: if no row was returned, issue ROLLBACK instead. Parameter $1 must be bound through the driver.

blocks.text: Parameterize values at the trusted boundary

Bind data values separately from SQL syntax. Parameters prevent a value from changing the query structure; they do not authorize the caller, validate business rules, or make dynamic identifiers safe. For table/column names that cannot be parameters, choose from a strict allowlist. Never concatenate untrusted input into a query.

steps.title: Keep query structure fixed
steps.explanation: The SQL text contains a placeholder; the driver binds the value separately rather than interpolating it into SQL.

steps.title: Apply authorization independently
steps.explanation: A safe parameterized query can still expose another user's row. Check the authenticated user's permission on the server/database policy.

options.text: The caller can only read their own rows
options.feedback: Authorization is a separate rule enforced by a trusted server or database policy.

options.text: The supplied value is treated as data, not SQL syntax
options.feedback: Bound parameters separate values from query structure; they do not grant or restrict access.

options.text: All dynamic table names are safe
options.feedback: Identifiers usually need strict allowlisting rather than value parameters.

options.text: The query always uses an index
options.feedback: Parameterization is a safety property, not a query-plan guarantee.

blocks.explanation: SQL safety, authorization, validation and performance are separate concerns.

blocks.prompt: Where should a filter such as COUNT(order_id) >= 2 go?

options.feedback: WHERE filters input rows; it cannot filter the aggregate result.
HAVING filters groups using aggregate values.
ORDER BY changes presentation order, not which groups qualify.
LIMIT bounds output rows but does not express an aggregate condition.

blocks.explanation: Separate row filters (WHERE) from group filters (HAVING).

blocks.title: Design a query from a reporting requirement
blocks.context: A dashboard needs one row per active customer, including those with zero purchases, plus the most recent purchase date.
instructions: Write a query that preserves active customers without purchase rows.
Return the number of purchases and latest timestamp.
Add a second version that returns only customers with at least three purchases.
Explain the result when a customer has no purchases and MAX(purchased_at) is NULL.
requirements: The result grain is one row per customer.
The join type preserves zero-purchase customers.
COUNT counts matched purchase IDs rather than the null-extended row.
HAVING is used only for the aggregate threshold.

blocks.prompt: Which predicate finds rows where deleted_at is missing?

options.feedback: Ordinary equality is not how SQL tests NULL.
IS NULL is the SQL predicate for a missing/unknown value.
undefined is a JavaScript value, not SQL syntax.
An empty string is different from NULL.

blocks.explanation: NULL handling changes query logic; do not replace it with empty strings or JavaScript values.

blocks.title: Query a small commerce schema safely
blocks.context: Use customers(id, name, active) and orders(id, customer_id, total, created_at) in a PostgreSQL practice database.
instructions: Return active customers and order counts including customers with zero orders.
Find customers with at least two orders and sort by count descending.
Select orders whose created_at value is NULL.
Describe how an API server should parameterize a user-provided customer ID.
Name an integrity constraint for orders.customer_id and explain why frontend filtering is not authorization.
requirements: The aggregate query uses an explicit join and grouping.
Zero-order customers are preserved when required.
NULL is tested with IS NULL/IS NOT NULL.
User input is parameterized, not concatenated into SQL.
Integrity constraints and authorization are distinguished.

items: Use JOIN and aggregation based on the schema relationships.
Handle NULL explicitly and use constraints to preserve integrity.
Parameterize input and enforce row access on the trusted server/data layer.
